name: Kerala coir craft
tagline: Coconut fibre craft that shaped Alappuzha’s economy and everyday life
summary: Traditional craft and industry turning coconut husk into ropes, mats, geo-textiles and handicrafts; Alappuzha is Kerala’s coir heartland with museums, workshops and continuing revival efforts.
description: Kerala coir craft is the traditional processing and hand- and machine-making of products from coconut husk fibre (coir). Alappuzha district and nearby coastal taluks are the historic and continuing production centre for matting, ropes, tufted mats, geo-textiles and garden articles.

The craft matters because it is both a living cottage industry and a community livelihood: government and cooperative agencies, local coir societies and private units provide work for large numbers of households — a high proportion of women workers — and feed value chains from local markets to exports.

Visitors get a close look at coastal retting pits, fibre extraction, hand-spinning, mat looms and tufting, plus the International Coir Museum at Kalavoor. You can buy simple raw-fibre goods, designer value-added items and small souvenirs directly from coir units and cooperative shops.
highlights: Alappuzha — Kerala’s long-established coir hub (many units and public-sector coir agencies).
Traditional stages: retting, fibre extraction, spinning, matting/tufting and finishing.
International Coir Museum (Kalavoor) explains history, techniques and mechanisation.
Range of products: ropes, door mats, tufted/handloom mats, coir pith, geotextiles and décor.
Active revival and training programmes run by state agencies and NCRMI.

sections.heading: Background
body: Coir making in Alappuzha grew from the district’s coconut-rich backwaters and the natural conditions for retting husks. Over the 20th century the sector expanded into many small units, coir co-operatives and a few public enterprises (Coirfed, Kerala State Coir Corporation, Foam Mattings). Government planning documents and sector agencies list Alappuzha as the nerve centre of Kerala’s coir economy.

sections.heading: How coir is made (materials & technique)
body: Raw material is coconut husk. Traditional retting uses backwater or lagoon water to rot the husks and loosen fibres; fibres are then separated, beaten/defibred, hand- or machine-spun into yarn, and woven or tufted into mats and rugs. Modern units also produce coir pith (growing medium) and geo-textiles for erosion control.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Visit the International Coir Museum at Kalavoor to learn the history, watch demonstration films and see tools and machinery. Walk through small coir workshops and co-operative showrooms in and around Alappuzha, where workers spin, weave and tuft; many places sell directly to visitors.

Look for value-added contemporary items — coir jewelry, planters, designer mats and eco-products — at coir federation outlets and local craft stores. If you can, arrange a short demonstration or a guided visit through a local coir society or NCRMI/KSCC outreach programme.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Coir activity functions year-round. Workshops are best seen during weekday working hours; the museum and cooperative showrooms have set opening hours (confirm before you travel). Local tourism offices and the International Coir Museum page give practical visitor details.

Buy directly from cooperative showrooms to support producers; ask about care instructions for coir products (sun-drying and occasional brushing help). If you plan to photograph workers or workshops, ask permission first.

latest.text: State launch in Alappuzha of the 'One House, One Coir Product' drive — minister-led door-to-door sales and a promotional push for coir items to boost demand and clear stock.
Kerala government announces a multi‑pronged strategy including a 'One Coir Product for Every Home' campaign and calls for district revival reports to rescue the crisis-hit coir sector.

visitorInfo.bestTime: October–February for pleasant weather; Onam season (Aug–Sep) for special campaigns and local sales events.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Alappuzha town is on NH66 and well connected by road and rail. Nearest major airport: Cochin International Airport (COK) with onward road/train connections. Local buses, taxis and hired autos reach coir villages and the Kalavoor museum.
etiquette: Confirm museum and workshop opening hours before you go.
Buy from cooperative outlets or workshops to ensure fair pricing; ask for care instructions.
Ask permission before photographing workers or close-up machinery.
If you visit retting areas, wear shoes and avoid wading — retting pits are not tourist bathing spots.
